correctness.rationale: For p_n(z)=-(1-z^n)^2/[2n(1-z)], von Neumann's inequality gives the contraction upper bound and multiplication by a maximizing scalar gives equality. A unit vector in ker(V*) produces an orthonormal orbit; normalized phase-modulated blocks on indices L through 2L-1 are weakly null and have (V-zI) residual sqrt(2/L) for |z|=1. Compact operators annihilate these vectors in norm in the limit, giving the full circle-supremum lower bound for distance to compacts and hence for all finite-rank distances (including k=1). On [pi/n,pi] the numerator of the modulus is at most 1 and the denominator is nondecreasing; a negative derivative at pi/n puts the maximum strictly in the first lobe for n>=2. There the logarithmic derivative is strictly decreasing from +infinity to a negative value, by sin(nu)<=n sin(u). This verifies the root equation and uniqueness on the stated interval (the two opposite phases are equivalent on the full circle). Uniform convergence after rescaling and a simple limiting root give x_n-x_*=O(n^-2); stationarity removes its first-order effect on the value. The expansion of x/(2n sin(x/(2n))) gives the displayed positive n^-2 coefficient with O(n^-4) remainder. Strong convergence follows by the mean ergodic theorem, or telescoping on ran(I-V) and density on the orthogonal complement of Fix(V).
residual_risks: Editorial precision: 'unique positive solution' refers to (0,pi), not all x>0. The exact correction coefficient is 0.1640680577938390313…, rather than the last displayed digit in the Finding; the exact expression is correct.

value.rationale: This canonical difference of consecutive dyadic Cesàro scales tends strongly to zero while retaining a nonzero sharp universal norm. Evaluating that norm, its finite-scale correction and the same obstruction after arbitrary compact perturbations gives a quantitative answer beyond standard qualitative mean ergodicity. The exact scalar reduction is standard, but the evaluated invariant is useful as a sharp bound and benchmark for comparisons of averaging schemes.
residual_risks: Not a full variational or square-function estimate, nor a rate for individual vectors; applicability is limited to the stated operator and hypotheses.
